lessons.title: Standings points and the loser point

payload.prompt: How many points does a team get for a regulation win?

options.text: One point
Two points
options.explanation: Correct. A regulation win is worth two points in the NHL standings.

options.text: Three points

explanation.correct: Right. Two points for a win, one point for an overtime loss, zero for a regulation loss.
explanation.incorrect: In the NHL, a regulation win is worth two points. Overtime losses earn one loser point.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two points for a win, one for losing in overtime.

payload.prompt: A team wins 35 games and loses 10. Estimate their points.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Thirty-five wins times two points equals seventy points.
explanation.incorrect: Each win is two points. Thirty-five times two is seventy. Regulation losses count as zero.
explanation.sayThisLine: Wins times two: that's your baseline points.

payload.prompt: Describe the loser point in the NHL standings.
payload.template: If a team loses in {{when}}, they get {{count}} point. It does not happen in {{where}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The loser point is an NHL quirk that does not exist in playoffs or the PWHL.
explanation.incorrect: The NHL gives one point for an overtime or shootout loss. The PWHL and playoffs do not use this rule.

payload.prompt: Two teams are tied on points. The team with more regulation wins gets the playoff spot. True or false?

scene.alt: Two teams with identical records competing for a playoff position.

explanation.correct: True. Regulation wins (RW) is the first tiebreaker when teams have the same points.
explanation.incorrect: When points are tied, you check regulation wins. That is the primary tiebreaker in the NHL standings.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tied on points? Check regulation wins first.

payload.prompt: Overtime in the regular season is 20 minutes of 3-on-3 play. True or false?

scene.alt: Three players per side competing in sudden-death overtime.

explanation.correct: False. Regular-season overtime is five minutes of 3-on-3, not twenty. It is sudden death.
explanation.incorrect: Regulation is three 20-minute periods. Overtime is five minutes, sudden death. First goal wins.
explanation.sayThisLine: Five minutes of 3-on-3 is all you get in the regular season.

payload.prompt: Describe why 3-on-3 creates scoring chances.
payload.template: With fewer players, there is {{space}} and {{time}} for each skater. The result is {{play}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Fewer skaters mean more space, and more space creates fast-paced, one-on-one situations.
explanation.incorrect: Three-on-three is chaotic because there is so much ice for each player. Breakaways are common.

payload.prompt: If neither team scores in overtime, what happens next?

options.text: Another overtime period
A shootout decides the game
options.explanation: Correct. If no goal in five minutes of 3-on-3, it goes to a best-of-three shootout.

options.text: The game is a tie

explanation.correct: Right. Five minutes of 3-on-3, then a shootout. No ties in the regular season.
explanation.incorrect: The regular season uses a shootout after five minutes of overtime. Playoffs go to multiple overtime periods.

payload.prompt: Match the advantage type to what it means in overtime.

pairs.definition: A fast player or team thrives in 3-on-3 because there is so much open ice.
A skillful skater or passer has more chances to make a play with fewer defenders.
After 60 minutes of regular play, tired legs can hurt in the breakaway-heavy overtime.

explanation.summary: Three-on-three rewards speed and skill while punishing poor conditioning. It is a different game.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three-on-three is all about speed and space.

lessons.title: The shootout
lessons.objective: Explain how it works and where it does not.

payload.prompt: Order how a shootout happens in the regular season.

items.text: Each team selects three skaters for the shootout.
items.why: Coaches choose their best shooters before the first round.

items.text: Teams alternate one-on-one shots at the goalie.
items.why: The first round is best-of-three: three shots per team, alternating.

items.text: If one team is winning after three rounds, they win the game.
items.why: If one team has more goals after round one, the game is over.

items.text: If tied after one round, sudden-death shooters go until one team scores and the other does not.
items.why: Sudden death: each team shoots one, and first team to win a round wins the game.

explanation.correct: Perfect. That is the shootout sequence: three rounds, then sudden death if needed.
explanation.incorrect: The shootout is three rounds of alternating shots, then sudden death. It is best-of-three initially.

payload.prompt: Does the Stanley Cup Playoffs use a shootout to decide games?

options.text: Yes, after five minutes of overtime
No, playoff games continue in multiple overtime periods until someone scores
options.explanation: Correct. The playoffs have no shootout; they keep playing 20-minute sudden-death periods.

options.text: Yes, but with five shooters per team

explanation.correct: Right. Playoffs are all-or-nothing: no shootout, just overtime until a goal is scored.
explanation.incorrect: The shootout is a regular-season tiebreaker only. Playoffs go to multiple overtime periods until there is a winner.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: We lost the shootout even though we had more shots on goal all game.

payload.question: What is the fan describing?

options.text: Luck in a one-on-one game is different from five-on-five play
options.explanation: Correct. The shootout is a different contest: it does not reflect regular play.

options.text: The other team's goalie was better overall
options.explanation: The fan is saying their team dominated but lost a shootout. That is a format issue, not a goalie issue.

options.text: The referees favored the other team
options.explanation: A shootout loss is about execution, not officiating.

payload.translation: The shootout is a skills contest, not a reflection of who controlled the game. You can dominate 5-on-5 and lose 1-on-1.

followUps.line: The shootout decides games but does not measure who played better. It is a gimmick by design.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the shootout's role as a tiebreaker, not a true test.

followUps.line: Some fans and experts think the shootout is unfair because it rewards something different than hockey.
followUps.why: Acknowledges the debate about shootout legitimacy.

followUps.line: Playoff hockey does not use shootouts, so only regular-season games are decided this way.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you think shootouts are unfair or a gimmick, that's a valid opinion that many fans share.

payload.prompt: A great sniper who excels at shootouts is a better all-around player than a grinder. True or false?

scene.alt: A skilled scorer preparing for a shootout attempt.

explanation.correct: False. Shootout skills are one narrow thing. A grinder's defensive work, effort, and team play matter across 60 minutes.
explanation.incorrect: The shootout is a one-on-one contest. Being good at it does not make you better at hockey overall. Different skills.

lessons.title: Wild cards and the playoff line

payload.prompt: Match the playoff position to what it means.

pairs.definition: The team with the most points in their division; automatically gets a playoff spot and hosts round one.
A non-division winner with enough points to make the playoffs; plays a division winner in round one.
A team that is not in the top three of their division and not a wild card; does not qualify.

explanation.summary: Sixteen teams make the NHL playoffs: three division winners plus two wild cards per conference.
explanation.sayThisLine: Top three in your division or grab a wild card spot.

payload.prompt: You are just outside the playoff line with two games left. What do you prioritize?

situation.narrative: Your team is three points behind the second wild card spot and has no realistic shot at a division title. You have two games remaining.

facts.label: Current position
facts.value: Fifth in division, three points out of wild card

options.label: Play all-out to try to make the playoffs
options.consequence: You give yourself a chance, but if you lose games, fans feel the season was wasted. A playoff miss after pushing hard is painful.
considerations: Playing hard at the end of the season keeps the culture strong
Selling out for a 15% chance is risky
Injuries can get worse if you push injured players

options.label: Rest key players and prepare for next season
options.consequence: You officially miss the playoffs but save star players from injury and get draft capital. Next season starts fresh.
considerations: Missing the playoffs is a coaching decision that fans debate harshly
Preserving cap space and youth development is smart long-term

options.label: Trade rentals and accept a rebuild
options.consequence: You get assets for next year, send a clear message about the rebuild, and gain cap flexibility. It stings now but builds for the future.
considerations: Trading stars late in the season can demoralize the locker room
Rentals are valuable at the deadline and can net solid prospects
The fanbase accepts a rebuild if it is clearly stated

payload.expertNote: At 15% odds with two games left, you are likely out. Smart teams at this point look to trade rentals, manage injuries, and build for next season. Pushing hard in games is fine, but converting roster assets to draft picks is the priority for a contender next year.
payload.sayThisLine: If the math says no, trade for the future.

payload.prompt: Describe how the NHL playoff bracket is built.
payload.template: The {{champ}} of each division make the playoffs, plus {{wc}} wild cards per conference, for {{total}} teams total.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Sixteen teams: three division winners and two wild cards per conference.
explanation.incorrect: The NHL playoffs have sixteen teams: three division winners per division and two wild cards per conference.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We are a wild card team, and wild cards face the division winner in round one. That is the matchup.

payload.question: What is the coach saying?

options.text: The team made the playoffs but did not win the division
options.explanation: Correct. Wild cards are playoff teams that did not finish top three in their division.

options.text: The team has a special card that lets them play anyone
options.explanation: Wild card is a playoff position, not a special card. It means you qualified without winning your division.

options.text: The team will play another wild card team first
options.explanation: Wild cards play division winners in round one, not other wild cards.

payload.translation: The team made the playoffs as a wild card (not a division winner), so in round one they face a division winner from their conference.

followUps.line: Wild cards are seeded against division winners, not against each other, so the matchups are predictable.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the playoff bracket structure.

followUps.line: Being a wild card can mean you face the most dominant team in your conference in round one.
followUps.why: Acknowledges that wild cards can get tough matchups.

followUps.line: A wild card that finishes second in points might face a weaker division winner, or vice versa.
followUps.why: Shows you understand that wild card placement does not guarantee an easy path.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Wild card seeding can be confusing at first. Look at the bracket to see who plays whom.

payload.prompt: Order the playoff rounds from first to last.

items.text: Round one: wild cards play division winners; 8 teams advance.
items.why: The first round of the playoffs starts with sixteen teams competing in eight series.

items.text: Round two: conference semifinals; eight teams play four series; four advance.
items.why: After round one, the eight winners move to the semifinals.

items.text: Round three: conference finals; four teams play two series; two advance.
items.why: The conference finals narrow the field to two teams per conference.

items.text: Finals: Stanley Cup Final; two teams compete for the Cup.
items.why: The last round is a best-of-seven for the Stanley Cup.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Four rounds of best-of-seven: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 champion.
explanation.incorrect: The playoffs have four rounds. Each round is a best-of-seven series; winners advance until one team wins the Cup.

payload.prompt: In a best-of-seven series, how many games must you win to advance?

options.text: Three games
Four games
options.explanation: Correct. The first team to four wins ends the series and advances.

options.text: Five games

explanation.correct: Right. Best-of-seven: first to four wins advances. The series can end in four, five, six, or seven games.
explanation.incorrect: A best-of-seven ends when one team wins four games. You cannot play more than seven games, but you can end early.

payload.prompt: Your team is down 3-1 in a playoff series with Game 7 tomorrow. How do you approach it?

situation.narrative: Your team is losing the series 3 games to 1. Game 5 was a close loss at home. One more loss and the season ends.

facts.label: Historical comeback
facts.value: Only 5 teams have come back from 3-1 in NHL history

facts.label: Team confidence
facts.value: Shaken but not broken after Game 5 loss

options.label: Play ultra-aggressive, go for broke
options.consequence: You might get an upset, but aggressive play often leads to mistakes and more goals against. Historical odds are against you.
considerations: Desperation play can work in one game but is risky over a series
Your opponent can counterattack if you overcommit offense
Fans will respect the effort even if you lose

options.label: Play your system and hope for bounces
options.consequence: Staying composed gives you the best shot at a Game 7, even if the odds are long. Discipline and focus beat panic.
considerations: Solid defense and discipline let you stay in games you should lose
A win in Game 6 shifts momentum and belief for Game 7
Playing your game is how underdogs steal series

options.label: Play to avoid embarrassment and gain draft position
options.consequence: Giving up demoralizes the team and fans. Even down 3-1, you play to win every game and make the opponent earn it.
considerations: Playing out the string poorly damages team culture
Draft position is not worth the locker-room damage
Pride and respect for the sport matter

payload.expertNote: Down 3-1, you are probably done, but you play Games 6 and 7 to win them. Bounces happen. If you lose, you lost playing hockey, not by quitting.
payload.sayThisLine: Down 3-1 is almost over, but you play to win until it is not.

payload.prompt: Home ice advantage in the playoffs means your team plays more games at home. True or false?

scene.alt: A rink packed with home fans cheering during a playoff game.

explanation.correct: True. Home ice means you host four games (2-2-1 format in a best-of-seven), so you play more at home.
explanation.incorrect: Home ice means you host more games. In a 2-2-1 series, the home team plays four at home and three away.
explanation.sayThisLine: Home ice is a real advantage: more games in your rink, your fans, your comfort.

lessons.title: The Stanley Cup
lessons.objective: Talk about the Cup and its traditions.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: The Stanley Cup is the most storied trophy in hockey. Every winner's name goes on it.

payload.question: What tradition is she describing?

options.text: Engraving: every winning player's name is added to the Cup permanently
options.explanation: Correct. The Stanley Cup is unique because it is engraved with every champion's name forever.

options.text: Each team gets a copy of the Cup to take home
options.explanation: There is one Stanley Cup in the vault, a replica for display, and a Presentation Cup. Names go on the real one.

options.text: Winners sell their name rights to the Cup
options.explanation: The Cup is not sold or licensed. Engraving a name is a historic honor.

payload.translation: The Stanley Cup is engraved with the name of every player, coach, and staff member who wins it. That permanence is what makes it iconic.

followUps.line: Players sometimes get the Cup for a day after winning to celebrate with family and friends. That is called 'having the Cup'.
followUps.why: Shows you understand the celebration tradition around winning.

followUps.line: The Stanley Cup has been awarded since 1893, so the engravings go back over a century.
followUps.why: Acknowledges the history and weight of the trophy.

followUps.line: The Cup is sometimes damaged or has wild parties, but that is part of its legend.
followUps.why: Shows respect for the tradition and the stories around it.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you do not know the Cup's traditions yet, asking about them is smarter than guessing a story.

payload.prompt: What trophy does the regular-season points leader get?

options.text: The Stanley Cup
The Presidents' Trophy
options.explanation: Correct. The Presidents' Trophy goes to the team with the best regular-season record, not the playoff champion.

options.text: The Hart Trophy

explanation.correct: Right. The Presidents' Trophy is for the best regular season. The Stanley Cup is for the playoff champion, which is different.
explanation.incorrect: The Presidents' Trophy rewards regular-season success. The Stanley Cup goes to the playoff winner. The best regular season does not guarantee the Cup.

payload.prompt: Order how a team wins the Stanley Cup.

items.text: Finish in the top three of your division or grab a wild card spot.
items.why: You need to make the playoffs first. Regular season puts you in position.

items.text: Win round one against a division winner or another wild card.
items.why: Four wins in a best-of-seven series advances you to the next round.

items.text: Win the conference semifinals against the other conference's survivors.
items.why: The second round narrows the field to four teams.

items.text: Win the conference final to reach the Stanley Cup Final.
items.why: Two teams are left: one per conference.

items.text: Win the Stanley Cup Final in a best-of-seven to claim the championship.
items.why: Four wins in the Cup Final means you are champions and your name goes on the trophy.

explanation.correct: Perfect. Sixteen teams, four rounds, one Stanley Cup champion. The playoff path is clear.
explanation.incorrect: The path to the Cup: make the playoffs, win four series (16 teams → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1), and claim it.

payload.prompt: Match the Cup tradition to what it means.

pairs.definition: Every player, coach and staff member who wins the Cup has their name added permanently to the trophy.
Winners get to take the Stanley Cup home for a day to celebrate with family, friends and their community.
The presentation of the Cup to the winning team on the ice, often with tears, hugs and celebration.

explanation.summary: The Stanley Cup has traditions that make winning it special and unforgettable. It is more than a trophy; it is a symbol.
explanation.sayThisLine: The Cup's traditions are what make it the greatest trophy in sport.
